questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was interested in trying out a Northern American campus culture in an international community. Vancouver seemed like an exciting and multicultural city, but the most important factor to me was the opportunity of exploring the beautiful nature in the western part of Canada.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It wasn't a big issue. Some information came pretty late but I never felt stressed out about it.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I moved into a residence on campus which was supported by local students. On our first day at campus, we had a full-day introductory program together with a small buddy group of other exchange students. The Go Global department at UBC was in general helpful to answer potential questions.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Information about housing on campus wasn't really sufficient but the orientation related to the study-part was pretty ok.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: As an exchange student, you can apply for housing on either Fairview Crescent or Walter Gage. I lived at Fairview Crescent, which is mainly 4-person apartments located in some kind of small village close to the forest. The atmosphere is super nice even though the houses are quite old. Walter Gage on the other hand is four high rises located centrally on campus with 6-person apartments.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: I've heard about some meal plans but it was too expensive, so I never really considered it.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
It's a great way to meet some new people. Both exchange students and local students! You need to buy pretty much everything yourself because UBC doesn't really offer any services when it comes to providing bed sheets, kitchen equipment etc... I would recommend reaching out to former exchange students in the Facebook group and asking if you can buy their sheets, towels, kitchen stuff etc. 

Housing on campus is significantly cheaper than most housing you can find outside the campus. Most people I talked to living off campus paid close to twice the price of what we paid. However, the campus is located a bit outside the city, so don't live there if you move to Vancouver to explore the big-city-vibe. Personally, I preferred the vibe on the campus compared to downtown, though.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had a great time living in residence on the campus and made some really good friends. However, I had a hard time understanding how UBC did nothing to help us with any of the things we needed to buy. We needed to buy router, laundry basket, hangers, sheets, towels, pillow, duvet, all kitchen equipment etc. ourselves just to through it out four months later (or try to get rid of it elsewhere). It would have been useful with some kind of recycling initiative from UBC. With that being said, I loved living on campus and will highly recommend it.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: As a graduate student in political science, you need to contact the professors directly to apply for a spot on their course. It was a messy process because I needed to hand in a course registration list to Go Global at UBC (because that is just how the procedure is for every exchange student) even though this was useless for them because they couldn't register you in any graduate courses. You can only apply for spots on the courses after the ordinary application process for the local student has ended but as soon as this period has ended you have to do it as quickly as possible (before the courses fill up). I was told that I couldn't apply for "restricted courses" as an exchange student, but almost every graduate course was restricted, and it wasn't a problem to get enrolled in them - so don't worry about applying for restricted courses.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Go Global (the exchange student department at UBC) was quick to answer any questions and helped me to figure out how to contact the professors on the different courses.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Partly successful. I did get some interesting courses but it was not among my top choices.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Just get in touch with the professors as soon as possible to get enrolled in the courses you find interesting. And remember that you can drop/add courses during the first weeks.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They had a bunch of interesting courses but most of them were full at the time I applied.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It varied quite a lot. I had one course with very high requirements. Almost half the students in the class were PhD-students and the professor expected a lot in terms of both reading and participation in the class. The other courses I had were more relaxed. Still, it was on a high academical level, but the workload was similar to what I know from KU.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It is quite different. Every class consists of 15-20 students and it is not run as a usual lecture but more interactive with a lot of student participation (participation is also a part of your final grade). The teacher expects you to participate, and during the semester I had several presentations. With that being said, you are not expected to come up with some very comprehensive arguments every time you take part in a discussion. I found most of the discussions more down to earth compared to most classes at KU.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Development Discourses and Practices
Developing Policies to Improve Population Health
Migration and Citizenship

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Developing Policies to Improve Population Health was a great course. It consisted of students from both political science and population health and it was very valuable to take a class together with people studying something different from myself. Also, Veena Sriram (the teacher in this course) is great! She has some other courses as well, and I'll highly recommend her.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I found it in general pretty expensive to live in Canada, but the biggest (unexpected) cost was all the weekend trips I did. There is so much to see and do in this area if you like exploring the nature, and it is not for free.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries (especially fresh and healthy food + alcohol) was more expensive than I expected. Gas and cars are cheap.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It's a paradise for those who love sports. They have gyms, an aquatic centre, a bunch of drop-in sports activities and so many different sports clubs to join. Also, remember to join VOC (Varsity Outdoor Club) if you are into outdoor things - they have a bunch of great trips and you can rent gear for free.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Pretty much everything you could imagine. Not that many targeted exchange students but it's rather easy to join the "normal" clubs and activities as an exchange student.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join VOC and make use of some of their nice trips if you are into outdoor things. Join one of the Thunderbird Sports Clubs if you like sports and want to make some Canadian friends. Go and watch some Thunderbird matches - especially Icehockey is nice.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go explore the nature around Vancouver, it's amazing. 
- Whistler is amazing for skiing in the winter and mountain biking in the summer. Make sure to buy a student season pass for Whistler. It's 600$ and a day ticket is up to 240$. 
- Squamish is amazing for climbing. 
- You have a lot of great hiking trails in the area that you can spend months exploring. 
- Vancouver Island is amazing, but go by car (or van) so you can explore more than just Victoria. Tofino is amazing for surfing and Campbell River is known as the salmon fishing capital of the world. 
- The Rockies are fantastic but make sure to have more time than just a weekend.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. Canadians are so friendly and they are used to welcoming people with different backgrounds.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join clubs on campus

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not really any I can think of.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How polite and friendly Canadians are.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Apply for housing on campus
2. Join some UBC clubs
3. Get out of the city and explore the nature

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not that I can think of

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Living together with people from other nationalities on campus and joining a UBC sports club

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I can think of a few even though none of them were huge. It was special to move to a place where you knew no one - especially in the beginning. Also, it took some time to get used to speaking academic English in class.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: UBC is a fantastic university and Vancouver and the nature surrounding it is absolutely amazing. I would highly recommend to almost everyone.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
